fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and it's actually the tension that has driven a lot of what my group has worked on over the past couple of years.

Let me start with the problem. The default choice for a long time has been to take a CLIP-style encoder, because contrastive training with captions gives you features that already live close to language. That makes alignment with the LLM easy; a small projector is enough. But the contrastive objective only asks the encoder to tell apart images at the level of a caption. It never needs to know exactly how many objects are there, what the small text in the corner says, or which way something is oriented. So those details get discarded, and you see it when you test the model on counting, OCR, spatial relations, or fine-grained categories. On the other side, self-supervised encoders like DINO or MAE keep a lot more of that local structure, but they have no notion of language, so people assumed they would be worse inside a multimodal model.

The first thing I'd say is that this trade-off is much less fundamental than it looked. In our work scaling language-free visual pretraining on web images, when we controlled for data distribution and pushed the model and data scale up, the self-supervised encoders caught up with CLIP on standard VQA and actually overtook it on the text-heavy and chart-style tasks. The LLM turns out to be a very good alignment mechanism by itself, as long as the visual features contain the information. So I would not treat language supervision in the encoder as a requirement. I'd treat it as one option, and the bigger levers are what images you train on and how many of them.

Given that, here is roughly how I'd design it. On data, make sure the pretraining distribution includes the hard cases, meaning documents, screenshots, dense scenes, text in the wild. Web images with text are a surprisingly large part of what moves the needle. On resolution, you need the encoder to operate at high or variable resolution, because fine-grained discrimination mostly dies at 224 pixels. That raises the question of token count, and this is where architecture matters. A plain ViT with a fixed patch size gives you a token budget that explodes with resolution. A hierarchical or convolutional design, which is where my ConvNeXt bias shows, lets you downsample spatially so the LLM sees fewer, richer tokens. You can also get there in a ViT with a pooling or compression stage before the projector, but you have to be careful not to pool away the detail you just paid for.

On which features to expose, don't only take the last layer. The last layer is the most semantic and the most compressed. Intermediate layers retain more local detail, and concatenating or fusing a couple of depths is a cheap way to serve both needs from a single network. I prefer that over bolting two different encoders together, which works but doubles your cost and tends to be a workaround for a pretraining problem.

Finally, don't freeze the encoder. A lot of the early recipes froze it to protect alignment, but joint training with a mixture that includes perception-heavy data lets the LLM pull the encoder toward whatever it is missing. And measure both axes separately. If you only look at aggregate VQA scores, you will not notice when your encoder forgets how to count.

r001.rationale: The response proposes preserving fine-grained visual information through self-supervised pretraining while using the LLM and joint multimodal training to provide language alignment, explicitly addressing both objectives.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or the use of world models in the vision component.

opus-5.5.text:
Language alignment and fine-grained discrimination pull in somewhat different directions, so I'd design with that tension in mind rather than assume one objective covers both.

The default today is a CLIP-style encoder, and there's a good reason for that. Contrastive image-text training gives you features that already live close to language, so connecting them to an LLM is relatively easy. But contrastive training only asks the model to learn whatever separates an image from the other captions in the batch. Captions are coarse. They say "a dog on a couch," not which way the dog is facing, how many legs are visible, or whether the text on the cushion says one thing or another. So the encoder is never pushed to keep those details, and often it doesn't.

We saw this directly in our work on what we called CLIP-blind pairs. We found pairs of images that look clearly different to a person but that CLIP embeds almost identically. Then we asked multimodal models simple questions about them: orientation, counting, viewpoint, whether something is present. The models failed in systematic ways, often near or below chance. The language model wasn't the problem. The information was already lost at the vision encoder, and no amount of LLM capacity downstream can recover it.

Self-supervised encoders like DINO-style models are almost the opposite. They're trained to be consistent and discriminative at the visual level, sometimes down to patches, with no captions involved. They keep much more spatial and structural detail. But their features aren't organized around language, so they're harder to align and weaker on semantic or knowledge-heavy questions.

So my design would have a few parts.

**Don't depend on a single caption-supervised objective.**
- **Mixing encoders.** The simplest version is to combine features from a language-supervised encoder and a self-supervised one before the projector. We tried interleaving them, and it improved visual grounding without giving up much on the language side.
- **One encoder, combined objectives.** The cleaner long-term version is a single encoder trained with a contrastive or captioning loss plus a dense self-supervised or reconstruction-type loss. The language loss gives you alignment, and the visual loss keeps the fine-grained information from being thrown away.

**Don't assume language supervision is required for good features.**
We've seen that if you scale self-supervised learning on the same kind of web-scale data CLIP uses, the visual features become competitive on many VQA-style tasks. That includes OCR and chart understanding, if the data has enough text-rich images. A lot of what we credited to language supervision was partly a data effect. Alignment can then come later, through the projector and joint training, rather than being baked into the encoder from the start.

**Treat resolution and tokens as first-class choices.**
Many fine-grained failures are just information bottlenecks:
- The image is downsampled to a low resolution.
- The spatial tokens are aggressively pooled.

You want higher-resolution inputs, through tiling or encoders that natively handle variable resolution. You also want to keep enough spatial tokens, or use a smarter aggregator that lets the LLM query the regions it needs, rather than compressing everything into a few global tokens up front.

**Don't freeze the encoder forever.**
Unfreezing it during later stages of multimodal training, with a careful learning rate, lets it adapt to what the downstream tasks actually need. That tends to help fine-grained ability without destroying alignment.

**Evaluate with vision-centric benchmarks.**
Many popular multimodal benchmarks can be partly solved by the language model's priors without really looking at the image. If you only measure those, you'll conclude the encoder is fine when it isn't. You need tests where the answer depends on visual detail: spatial relations, counting, depth, orientation, small text. Ideally they should be built so a blind LLM can't guess them.

To sum up: use language supervision for alignment, but don't let it be the only signal shaping the representation. Add a strong visual objective, preserve resolution and spatial information, and measure the model on tasks where it actually has to look.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or the use of world models for the vision component.

fable-5.text:
Thanks, Ravid — it's great to be here. That's a question I think about a lot, because those two goals are genuinely in tension, and most of the field's default choices quietly favor one over the other.

The standard recipe is to take a CLIP-style encoder, because contrastive training against text captions gives you features that already live close to language space — the alignment problem becomes almost trivial. But captions are a lossy description of an image. If the caption never mentions which way the arrow points or how many legs the chair has, the contrastive objective has no incentive to preserve that information. So you get an encoder that's wonderful at semantic categories and surprisingly blind to fine-grained structure — text in images, counting, spatial relations, small object differences. Benchmarks probing visual details have made this failure mode pretty obvious.

So if I were designing from scratch, I'd do a few things. First, don't rely on a single objective. Combine the contrastive, language-aligned signal with something dense and self-supervised — a masked reconstruction or DINO-style objective — so the features are forced to retain information the captions don't mention. A practical shortcut people use is fusing features from two encoders, one CLIP-like and one DINO-like, and that works, but I'd rather bake both pressures into one model.

Second, resolution matters enormously for fine-grained discrimination, and I'd want native flexibility there — either an architecture that handles variable resolutions gracefully, which is actually a place where convolutional or hybrid designs have an edge over vanilla ViTs, or a tiling scheme so you're not stuck at 336 pixels.

Third, don't freeze the encoder. Unfreezing it and training jointly with the language model on interleaved data lets the LLM's next-token loss pull out details the pretraining objective ignored. The alignment doesn't have to be fully solved at pretraining time — it can be finished during joint training, as long as the information is still in the features. That's really the core principle: alignment you can fix later, but information you've thrown away is gone.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes combining language-aligned contrastive training with dense self-supervised objectives during encoder design/pretraining to preserve fine-grained visual information.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or the use of world models in the vision component.

opus-5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we actually ran into empirically, and my honest answer is that you probably shouldn't expect one encoder to do both well.

The way most of these models are built, you take CLIP, or something CLIP-like, because the whole point is that the representation already lives in a space that's been shaped by language. That makes the alignment problem almost trivially easy — you can get away with a tiny connector and not much data. But when we started poking at failure cases, we found pairs of images that are obviously different to any person, and CLIP embeds them almost identically. Orientation of an object, whether a flag is pointing left or right, how many of something there are. And then the multimodal model inherits that blindness exactly. The language model isn't the bottleneck there; the information is already gone before the LLM ever sees it. And it doesn't go away with scale, which I think is the uncomfortable part. We tried bigger CLIP models, more data, higher resolution — the specific blind pairs persist.

Meanwhile the self-supervised models, DINOv2 and friends, are quite good at precisely those distinctions, because nothing in their objective is pushing them to throw away details that language rarely mentions. But they're not language-aligned, so if you just swap one in you pay a real cost on instruction following and general VQA.

So concretely, what I'd do: use both. And the detail that mattered more than I expected is *how* you combine them. If you just blend the features additively, you get a dial — more DINOv2 helps on fine-grained discrimination, hurts on the language-y benchmarks, and you're trading. If instead you interleave the tokens spatially, so the LLM sees both views and can attend to whichever it needs, you get a lot of the visual gain without giving up the instruction following. The LLM turns out to be fairly flexible about consuming heterogeneous visual tokens.

And then I'd say: be careful what you measure. Most benchmarks let a strong language prior paper over visual failures. You need evaluations built from pairs that are visually distinct but textually confusable, otherwise you'll convince yourself the encoder is fine when it isn't.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes using both a language-aligned CLIP-like encoder and a self-supervised encoder such as DINOv2, combining their visual representations to retain alignment and fine-grained discrimination.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or the use of world models for the vision component.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'd start by questioning whether the encoder itself has to do both jobs. The usual assumption is that it should be language-aligned, which is why CLIP and SigLIP became the default. But that kind of supervision has a cost. Captions describe the gist of an image, so the model never gets much pressure to preserve fine-grained detail like exact spatial relationships, counting, or small textures. That's where you get the "CLIP blind spots," where two images look clearly different to a vision model but get nearly identical embeddings.

On the other side, self-supervised models like DINOv2 keep that fine-grained, vision-centric information, but they weren't trained against language. For a long time, people took that as a reason not to use them in multimodal models.

In our work on Cambrian, we found it's more nuanced. If you evaluate a wide range of encoders inside an MLLM, language-supervised ones do better on knowledge-heavy and OCR-style tasks, and self-supervised ones do better on vision-centric tasks. Combining them helps. We built a spatial vision aggregator that lets the LLM query features from several encoders at once. That's one practical recipe, and the cost is complexity and compute.

My preferred direction is to make the visual representation itself stronger and let the LLM and connector handle the alignment. In our recent work on scaling language-free visual representation learning, we trained purely visual SSL models at larger scale, up to several billion parameters, on web-scale data. Two things stood out. First, performance kept improving with scale, where it had seemed to saturate before. Second, the data distribution mattered a lot. When we included more text-rich images, the models got much better at OCR and chart understanding, closing most of the gap to CLIP, even though there was no language supervision. So the old claim that you need language supervision for those capabilities looks more like a data issue than a fundamental limit.

So if I were designing it today, I'd do four things:

- **Train a large visual encoder with SSL on diverse, web-scale data**, including a meaningful share of text-heavy images.
- **Use high or flexible resolution**, because fine-grained discrimination partly depends on not throwing pixels away.
- **If I wanted language alignment inside the encoder, add it as one objective among several**, as in SigLIP 2, rather than the only objective. That means contrastive plus dense or self-distillation losses, not contrastive alone.
- **Evaluate with vision-centric benchmarks**, not just general VQA. Many VQA questions can be answered mostly from language priors, which hides the weaknesses of the visual side.

If I had to pick one thing, it would be scaling and curating the data for a visual-only encoder, because that gets you fine-grained features without giving up the semantic and text-reading abilities the LLM needs.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes combining language alignment with fine-grained visual learning, via large-scale SSL on diverse data and optionally adding language alignment as one objective alongside dense or self-distillation losses.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or the use of world models in the vision component.

haiku-5.5.text:
That's a tension I keep coming back to. The standard recipe, contrastive image-text pretraining, gives you features that already sit close to language, which is exactly what alignment needs. But that objective mostly rewards a global summary. The model learns that the caption matches the picture, and it has little reason to preserve where a small object is or how many of something there are. Fine-grained detail often gets sacrificed for that alignment.

I wouldn't treat these as two separate encoders. I'd start with a strong language-aligned backbone and add dense supervision on the patch tokens, not just the pooled embedding. Region-level or grounding-style objectives keep spatial information alive. Resolution is the other big lever. Many failures on fine-grained questions come down to the encoder seeing too few pixels per object, so I'd support high or native resolution, through tiling or a resolution-flexible design. I'd also let the language model consume the full spatial token grid rather than one pooled vector.

Token budget is the real constraint. Dense features at high resolution get expensive quickly, so I'd compress thoughtfully, with learned pooling or token merging in later layers, rather than throwing away resolution up front.

On training, I'd keep alignment as the main objective but add a stage that emphasizes localization and counting. And I'd check those abilities directly. If your evaluations only cover captioning and general VQA, you won't notice that you've lost the fine detail.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly combines language alignment with fine-grained visual discrimination by retaining a language-aligned backbone while adding dense patch/region supervision and localization/counting objectives during training.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or world models; it focuses on spatial tokens, resolution, grounding, and token compression.

astra-6.text:
I would start by recognizing that language alignment and visual discrimination ask for somewhat different things. Language tells you which aspects of an image are useful to describe, but it doesn’t necessarily capture every visual detail. Two images can have the same caption and still look quite different.

So I’d use a shared vision backbone with two complementary training objectives. One would align visual representations with text. The other would encourage the encoder to preserve distinctions between images and between local regions, without requiring those distinctions to be expressed in words. I’d give those objectives separate projection heads so that the representation used for language alignment doesn’t have to carry every detail in exactly the same form.

For the language model, I’d retain spatial patch features rather than passing only a pooled image representation. That gives it access to both the overall semantics and the local evidence needed for fine-grained questions.

The important test is whether both capabilities survive multimodal training. I’d evaluate language grounding and fine-grained visual discrimination separately, because improving the language-facing benchmark alone wouldn’t tell us whether the encoder is still preserving useful visual information.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes a shared vision backbone with complementary objectives for visual-text alignment and preserving fine-grained distinctions between images and local regions.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or the use of world models in the vision component.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with a vision encoder that preserves rich visual information, and then build language alignment on top of that. Those objectives overlap, but they’re not identical. A caption usually describes only a small fraction of what’s in an image. If you train entirely around matching that caption, there’s little incentive to preserve details like texture, precise spatial relationships, or small differences between similar objects.

So I would combine an image-based self-supervised objective with an image–text alignment objective. The first encourages the backbone to retain visual structure; the second makes that representation accessible to language. A separate projection layer gives you some flexibility: the features used for language alignment don’t have to be exactly the same features you use for fine-grained discrimination.

I’d also preserve spatial tokens rather than compressing the whole image into one vector. Depending on the task, higher-resolution inputs or multiple scales could help the language model access small objects and local details. Of course, that introduces a token and compute budget, so the connector needs to select or compress information carefully.

Finally, I would evaluate both capabilities explicitly. Better image–text matching doesn’t automatically mean better visual discrimination. You want to check whether the model can actually distinguish similar instances, recognize attributes, and resolve spatial relationships while still following language instructions.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes combining an image-based self-supervised objective for retaining fine-grained visual structure with an image–text alignment objective.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or the use of world models in the vision component.

sol-6.text: I’d design it around two needs. The language model needs a compact representation that captures what an image means, but it also needs access to local details when the question depends on a small object, text, or a subtle difference. So I’d use a vision encoder that preserves features at multiple scales: a small set of global tokens for language alignment and finer spatial tokens for detailed inspection. During training, I’d combine image–text alignment with tasks that require grounding and discrimination between similar images or regions. Then I’d let the model select the detailed tokens it needs, so it doesn’t pay the cost of processing every patch for every question.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly combines image–text alignment with grounding and discrimination tasks for similar images or regions, addressing both language alignment and fine-grained visual discrimination.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or world models; it discusses multiscale spatial features and token selection instead.

terra-5.6.text:
I think the key is not to treat those two goals as exactly the same objective. Language alignment wants invariance: if two images can be described with the same words, the encoder is encouraged to put them close together. But fine-grained discrimination often needs the opposite—you need to preserve the small differences between, say, two bird species or two instances of the same object.

So I would use a high-resolution, hierarchical vision backbone that keeps local spatial features, rather than compressing everything immediately into a single global token. Then I’d align a semantic, global representation with language, while retaining patch-level or multi-scale visual tokens for the language model to attend to when it needs detail. Training should also include objectives that preserve visual distinctions—dense or region-level supervision, hard negatives, and perhaps self-supervised reconstruction or discrimination—rather than relying only on image-text contrastive loss.

In other words, you want a shared semantic space for communication with language, but you don’t want that interface to destroy the rich visual representation underneath it.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes jointly supporting language alignment and fine-grained visual discrimination through semantic alignment plus preserved patch-level features and distinction-preserving training objectives.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or world models for the vision component.

sol-5.6.text:
I would avoid forcing a single supervision signal to do both jobs. Language-aligned objectives, like CLIP, give you strong semantic features, but they tend to discard details that are not useful for matching captions. Self-supervised vision models preserve much richer local structure, but their features are harder for a language model to use.

So I’d train one encoder to distill from both kinds of teachers: a language-aligned teacher for global semantic alignment and a vision-only teacher for fine-grained spatial discrimination. I’d keep both patch-level and global features, use separate projection heads so the objectives do not fight unnecessarily, and train across multiple image resolutions so the representation remains useful for dense tasks and high-resolution inputs. The result is a single shared backbone that can feed an MLLM while retaining the visual detail needed for recognition, localization, and other fine-grained tasks.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes training one vision encoder with both a language-aligned teacher for semantic alignment and a vision-only teacher for fine-grained spatial discrimination.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose temporal modeling or the use of world models; it discusses spatial features, resolutions, and teacher distillation instead.

luna-5.6.text:
I would use a hierarchical, multi-scale encoder with two complementary outputs. One would be a compact set of global tokens, optimized for semantic alignment with language; the other would preserve dense, high-resolution regional tokens for details such as text, object attributes, and spatial relationships.

The global branch could be trained with image–text contrastive and captioning objectives, while the local branch receives region-level grounding, OCR, and fine-grained discrimination losses. I would share an early visual backbone, but allow the two branches to specialize later, since the features that are ideal for matching “a dog on a beach” are not necessarily the ones needed to distinguish breeds or read small text.

For the language model interface, I would use a learned resampler or cross-attention module with adaptive token selection: simple images produce fewer visual tokens, while cluttered or detail-heavy images retain more local information. I would also preserve positional and multi-scale information rather than pooling everything into a single embedding. The key is to make global alignment efficient without forcing the encoder to discard the local evidence required for precise visual reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly combines language alignment objectives (image–text contrastive and captioning) with fine-grained visual discrimination objectives (region grounding, OCR, and attribute/detail preservation) in a two-branch vision encoder.

luna-6.text: I’d avoid asking one representation to do everything. Start with a strong pretrained vision encoder, but keep its spatial features rather than collapsing the image into a single embedding. For language alignment, train a global representation to capture the objects and relationships people describe. For fine-grained discrimination, preserve higher-resolution, multi-scale features so the model can still tell apart details like a small object, a texture, or a subtle attribute. Then connect those features to the language model through a learned projection, and train with both image–text alignment and tasks that require precise visual answers. The key is to align the representation with language without throwing away the visual information that language may need to ask about later.
